extracted.intended_audience: health care journalists and public relations/communications professionals who write or evaluate health-related press releases
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for writing and evaluating press releases about health care, clinical research, and medical interventions to align with principles of accurate, responsible health journalism. Emphasizes accuracy, transparency, quantification of benefits/harms, disclosure of conflicts, and contextualization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professionalism, Content, and Accuracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Accuracy is paramount; distinguish facts from opinion; distinguish correlation from causation; avoid sensational language; acknowledge uncertainty; quantify benefits and harms; disclose conflicts of interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This high-level principle requires all reporting and release language to be factually verifiable, careful about causal claims, and restrained in tone. Quantification and transparency about uncertainty are core components; conflicts must be disclosed up front.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independence
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain editorial independence from sources; resist pressure from advertisers; don't accept gifts/junkets that create conflicts; disclose sponsorships.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Press releases (and the journalists who use them) should not let funders, advertisers, or hospitality influence claims or framing. Any sponsorship or material support must be clearly disclosed so readers can judge potential bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrity
rubrics_metrics.description: Cite sources; identify experts honestly; note conflicts of interest of sources; verify claims independently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Name data sources (studies, datasets), give accurate expert affiliations and roles, call out relevant financial or professional ties of quoted experts, and where possible corroborate claims with independent evidence or comment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider impact on patients; avoid creating false hope or fear; place findings in context; provide actionable information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how wording could influence patient decisions or expectations. Avoid hype that could cause unnecessary alarm or unrealistic expectations; instead offer context about what readers can reasonably do or expect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verifiable facts only
rubrics_metrics.description: Press releases should include only facts that can be verified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid speculative assertions presented as facts. Where data or claims are preliminary, label them as such and provide source details (study citation, link to preprint, raw numbers) so claims can be checked.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish associations from causation
rubrics_metrics.description: Clearly separate correlational findings from causal claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a study is observational or otherwise unable to establish causality, the release must state that associations do not prove cause-and-effect and explain what kind of evidence would be needed for causal inference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific (not vague) claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Use specific language rather than vague or ambiguous statements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide concrete measures, populations, time frames, and effect sizes instead of generic claims like "helps" or "may improve" without quantification and scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cite peer-reviewed source
rubrics_metrics.description: Cite and link to the peer-reviewed study or clearly label non–peer-reviewed sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When possible, provide a full citation and link to the peer-reviewed article. If the work is a preprint, press release should explicitly state that and note the lack of peer review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Note study design limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Report study design (randomized trial, observational, preclinical) and its limitations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State sample characteristics, control/comparison conditions, blinding, randomization status, and other design features; explain how these affect interpretation and generalizability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid sensational language
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use terms like "breakthrough", "cure", or unverified "first" claims; avoid sensational or hyperbolic wording.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Restrict superlatives unless unequivocally supported; use measured language and precise statistical terms. Prefer absolute statistics over headline-grabbing relative ones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use precise statistics (absolute numbers)
rubrics_metrics.description: Report absolute risks and absolute effect sizes rather than only relative risks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide baseline rates, absolute risk reduction, and where applicable number-needed-to-treat. Present frequencies (e.g., "5 of 100") alongside percentages for clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge uncertainty
rubrics_metrics.description: Include confidence intervals, sample size, generalizability limits, and replication status.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quantify uncertainty (CIs, p-values when appropriate), say how large the study was and whether results have been replicated. Be explicit about limits to extrapolating findings to other populations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantify benefits and harms
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide absolute risk reduction, number needed to treat, side-effect frequencies, and costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report both benefits and harms with frequencies and magnitudes. Avoid presenting only benefit-oriented metrics that exaggerate perceived effects; include likely costs and burdens if relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclose conflicts of interest (COIs) and funding
rubrics_metrics.description: Disclose funding sources, industry ties of researchers, patents/financial interests, and sponsoring organizations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: List study funders, corporate affiliations, consulting fees, equity interests, patents or licensing arrangements, and any other material ties that could influence study design, interpretation, or messaging.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide context
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare findings with existing treatments/knowledge, indicate the current standard of care, cost-benefit considerations, and available alternatives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Help readers understand where a finding fits into the broader evidence base: is it incremental, confirmatory, or contradictory? Note clinical relevance relative to current options and practical considerations like access and cost.

rubrics_metrics.name: All claims verifiable
rubrics_metrics.description: Every claim in the release should be capable of verification against cited data or sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include citations, links, or references for empirical claims. Avoid anecdote-as-evidence; label unsupported or hypothetical statements as such.

rubrics_metrics.name: Causal vs correlational distinguished (implicit rubric)
rubrics_metrics.description: Explicitly flag when results are correlational rather than causal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain limitations of observational designs and the additional evidence required to support causal inference (e.g., randomized trials, mechanistic evidence).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sample size and design noted (implicit rubric)
rubrics_metrics.description: State the sample size and key design features of the study.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report n, recruitment method, inclusion/exclusion criteria, follow-up duration, and whether analyses were pre-specified. Small or convenience samples require cautious framing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect sizes in absolute terms (implicit rubric)
rubrics_metrics.description: Report effect sizes in absolute terms, not only relative percentages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a release cites percent changes, also provide concrete baseline and post-intervention numbers so readers can assess practical impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidence intervals included (implicit rubric)
rubrics_metrics.description: Include confidence intervals (or other uncertainty estimates) for reported effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide CIs to show statistical precision; avoid implying certainty when estimates are imprecise or cross null values.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harms quantified (implicit rubric)
rubrics_metrics.description: Report harms and adverse events with frequency information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: List common and serious side effects with numeric frequencies; clarify which adverse events are causally linked versus temporally observed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Funding disclosed (implicit rubric)
rubrics_metrics.description: State who funded the research or press release.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make funder names prominent; if funders had a role in study design, data analysis, or manuscript preparation, disclose that role.

rubrics_metrics.name: COIs disclosed (implicit rubric)
rubrics_metrics.description: Declare conflicts of interest for investigators and organizations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: List investigator financial interests and institutional relationships that could bias conduct or interpretation; disclose press release authorship and any PR firm involvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Context vs alternatives provided (implicit rubric)
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide comparison with existing options and plausible alternatives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain how the finding compares to standard treatments, lifestyle options, or other interventions; mention if more-effective or cheaper alternatives exist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations acknowledged (implicit rubric)
rubrics_metrics.description: State study and generalization limitations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Call out small samples, short follow-up, surrogate endpoints, animal/preclinical status, or potential confounding biases that limit applicability.

rubrics_metrics.name: No sensational language (implicit rubric)
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid hype, exaggeration, and hyperbolic headlines or claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use cautious headlines and avoid framing that implies definitive cure or breakthrough when evidence is preliminary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provides reader-actionable information (implicit rubric)
rubrics_metrics.description: Give readers clear, appropriate actions or advice when applicable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the information implies behavior change or clinical decisions, state what is currently recommended and whether readers should consult clinicians; avoid prescriptive advice beyond the evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cites peer-reviewed source (implicit rubric)
rubrics_metrics.description: Include citation or link to peer-reviewed publication when available.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If peer review is pending or absent, clearly label the work (preprint, conference abstract) and note implications for confidence in the findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguishes hypothetical from observed (implicit rubric)
rubrics_metrics.description: Make clear what is hypothetical, modeled, or speculative versus what was actually observed in the study.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Label modeling, projections, or mechanistic hypotheses explicitly; separate them from empirical results and report their assumptions and limitations.
